notes.meaning: Elihu pauses for a moment to see if Job will offer a reply. When Job remains quiet, Elihu takes up the conversation once again.
Elihu addresses the other listeners around him, calling them wise and educated men. Even though he disagrees with Job's friends, he treats them with courtesy and asks them to weigh his words.
Elihu repeats a well-known proverb that Job had mentioned earlier. Just as the mouth can taste different foods, the mind must test words to see which ones are true and wholesome.
Elihu invites the group to work together to find what is right. He urges them not to argue merely to win, but to unite in discovering God's true standard of goodness.
Elihu summarizes Job's previous complaints. He points out that Job claimed to be in the right, while insisting that God had taken away his fair day in court.

Job had refused to falsely admit guilt just to please his companions, saying that would be lying about his record. He felt his terrible wound could not be healed, even though he had done nothing wicked to deserve it.

Elihu strongly rebukes Job, asking where another man can be found who drinks down mocking words as easily as water. He believes Job has allowed himself to take pleasure in speaking disrespectfully about God's ways.
Elihu charges Job with acting like an ally of wicked people. He does not mean Job lived a lawless life, but that Job's bitter complaints mirrored the exact arguments that godless men use.

Elihu claims Job said that delighting in God brings no lasting advantage to a person. While Job never said those exact words, Elihu drew this conclusion because Job complained that the righteous and the wicked suffer the same fate.
Elihu calls on sensible listeners to agree on a bedrock truth: God can never do evil. Because the Almighty is totally pure, doing wrong or twisting justice is impossible for Him.
Elihu states that God repays every person according to their conduct. Even if justice is not fully carried out in this present life, God will certainly give everyone their due in the end.
Elihu repeats with deep conviction that God will never act wickedly. The Almighty will never deny any person their rights or pervert justice.
Elihu asks who gave God authority over the earth. God did not receive the world from a superior ruler, but created it Himself, meaning He has no selfish motive to harm His own creation.

If God were to think only of Himself and withdraw His life-giving breath, every living creature would immediately die. All humanity would crumble back into dust at once. The fact that God sustains our life proves He is not uncaring or unjust.
Elihu turns his attention back to Job. He urges Job to use his understanding and listen carefully to the next part of the argument.

Elihu asks how someone who hates fairness could possibly rule the universe. True leadership requires justice, so it is unthinkable for a human to condemn the One who is both all-powerful and perfectly right.
Ordinary people would never dare look an earthly king in the eye and call him corrupt or worthless. If human rulers receive such honor, a person should be far more careful about accusing God.
God shows no favoritism to powerful leaders and does not care more for the rich than the poor. He treats every person with equal fairness because He created them all.
The most powerful leaders can perish in an instant, even in the middle of the night. God removes them without human armies or weapons, showing that worldly strength cannot stand before Him.
God keeps His eyes on everything humans do and notices every step they take. Nothing in a person's life is hidden from His view.
There is no darkness or deep shadow thick enough to conceal evildoers from God. While people may hide their sins from their neighbors, God sees everything clearly.

God does not need to set a special trial date or spend extra time investigating someone before rendering judgment. Because He already knows the whole truth, His verdicts are instant and completely fair.
God breaks mighty rulers to pieces without needing lengthy hearings. He easily sweeps corrupt rulers away and places others in their positions.
Because God already knows their secret plots, He overthrows oppressors suddenly under the cover of night. Their authority is shattered before they even realize what is happening.
God punishes wicked rulers openly where the public can witness it. This visible judgment proves to everyone that God will not let wrongdoing go unchecked.

These leaders were overthrown because they refused to follow God and showed no regard for His ways. Their cruel treatment made the poor and afflicted cry out in distress, and God heard their pleas for help.
When God gives peace to an individual or a nation, no enemy can stir up real trouble. But if He hides His favor in judgment, no one can demand to see Him or overturn His decree.
God removes corrupt leaders so that ungodly men cannot continue to rule and trap the people in suffering. He watches over nations to protect ordinary citizens from oppressive traps.

Elihu explains what a suffering person should say to God. Instead of complaining, one should humbly accept correction, ask God to reveal any unrecognized sins, and resolve to turn away from wrong in the future.
Elihu asks whether God should govern the world on Job's terms. Since Job rejected the way God handles things, Elihu challenges Job to propose a better plan if he can.
Elihu claims that any sensible person listening will agree with his assessment. They will conclude that Job has spoken without true knowledge and that his complaints lack wisdom.
Elihu desires that Job's trial through hardship continue until his pride is broken. He makes this harsh wish because he believes Job has answered just like wicked men who fight against God.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Earlier Latin commentators translated the opening word as an appeal to God ('My Father'), though traditional Catholic expositors like Gregory the Great also noted that Elihu spoke with personal pride.

notes.meaning: Elihu concludes that Job has added stubborn rebellion to his earlier grief. He accuses Job of clapping his hands in defiance against his friends and pouring out endless words against God.
